READING PASSAGE 1 
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1-13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 
on pages 2 and 3. 
 
How deserts grow  
In the 1930s, the United States entered an economic disaster. Farmers in western areas had 
been plowing the plains for land that had long been covered naturally by native grass. Without 
the natural grass to hold the soil together, strong winds lifted dust into the air. The resulting 
huge dust storms led to long periods of dust blowing in many places. The Dust Bowl, as this 
period of great environmental damage became known, was a lesson about desert formation 
through a combination of nature and human action. 
 
Deserts are spreading in many regions like the western United States. large portions of northern 
Africa, Central Asia and Latin America face the real problem today. When we think of deserts, 
we may see only sand, but deserts can take many different forms, including dry grassland and 
dry woodland. When hot dry winds blow day after day, the soil becomes poor and unable to hold 
moisture in any form. When soil loses the balance of sustainability, the result is desertification, 
dry land turning into desert ecosystems. Nearly half of the world’s total land mass is composed 
of dry land ecosystems, defined by low annual rainfall and high temperatures. It was reported 
that up to 20% of these regions are already degraded and unsuitable for human, animal or plant 
life. 
 
Dryland regions are also home to billions of the world’s poorest populations. Desertification 
leads to famine and extremely high levels of human migration. As people are displaced by new 
deserts, they are forced into other infertile regions, where the desertification process continues. 
Desertification is one of the world’s most urgent environmental issues, but it is not irreversible. 
Years after the Dust Bowl, federal conservation programs were able to restore the Great Plains 
to fertility. 
 
In a healthy dryland ecosystem, relatively few animals and humans attempt to survive on the 
limited resources of the land, such as water, fertile soil and trees. Since rainfall is infrequent in 
semiarid regions, the land is not built to support huge fields of crops or to supply grazing for 
hundreds of thousands of cattle. The root cause of desertification is poor soil conditions leading 
to soil degradation. Healthy, productive soil is rich with organic matter. Humus is formed when 
rotted organic materials are transformed by micro organisms and fungi in soil that is rich in 
essential elements. Planting different crops on a piece of land each season, and responsible 
use of chemical fertilizers ensure that the soil has enough organic input to support healthy micro 
organisms. When topsoil is depleted of humus, it is either too loose or too compacted, both of 
which can lead to destructive erosion. All the rain in the world will not help infertile topsoil; it will 
only wash away. 
 
Perhaps the greatest cause of soil erosion and desertification is an explosion in world 
population, particularly in developing countries. Throughout the 1980s, dry regions in developing 
countries, many expanding in desperately poor, developing countries, experienced huge

3 
 
population growth. Poor human populations have put a deadly strain on natural resources. 
Increasing numbers of people mean increased numbers of grazing animals and increased 
demand for firewood for fuel, exposing the topsoil to destructive erosion. Firewood is also used 
for cooking by many people. When unchecked, over cutting of forests by poor populations leads 
to increasing dry land desertification and slowing down the water cycle. 
 
Human activities also worsen the biggest problem of living in a dryland region: lack of rainfall. 
When land is cleared of plant life, from overgrazing or logging, the surface of the Earth reflects 
more sunlight up into the atmosphere, creating even hotter temperatures. In semi arid regions, 
higher temperatures cause a higher rate of evaporation, and even less rainfall. The dust kicked 
up by cattle and the smoke created by wildfires introduce heavy particles into the atmosphere, 
making it more difficult for raindrops to form. Even war contributes to desertification. When 
refugees flee from invading armies, they move into some of the most marginal ecosystems in 
the world, bringing with them their farming practices, which can be highly unsuitable for their 
new home. 
 
Ninety percent of the people who live in dryland ecosystems — those areas most prone to soil 
degradation and desertification — are citizens of developing countries. This adds up to billions 
of people, mostly poor and marginalized, who are immediately affected by the deadly 
consequences of desertification. Experts estimate that more than 24,000 people die every day 
from the effects of desertification. It is estimated that more than 70% of drylands in Africa, Asia 
and Latin America which are used for agricultural purposes are already experiencing these 
effects, it is time to start addressing this problem by educating the whole range of causes.
